1 big thing: The AI bubble refuses to pop for Anthropic
By Madison Mills and Dan Primack
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Anthropic blew past its expected IPO price range yesterday, raising more than $80 billion in a historic listing that showed the AI boom is far larger — and appears more resilient — than the fate of a single chipmaker or its CEO.

Why it matters: Despite weeks of existential dread in the industry following a scandal that took down Nvidia's Jensen Huang, Anthropic's higher-than-expected pricing offered a strong signal that investor appetite for frontier AI is robust enough to survive serious structural shocks.

Zoom in: Anthropic priced its long-awaited IPO at $83 per share, giving the Claude maker an initial market cap of $1.08 trillion and a fully diluted value of around $1.5 trillion.

  • Anthropic originally planned to sell 825 million shares but increased to 980 million shares.
  • The company also could raise significantly more money if underwriters exercise their so-called "greenshoe" option, while Anthropic also will receive $26 billion via a concurrent private placement from tech giants like Nvidia, Google and Microsoft.

Context: Anthropic was valued at $965 billion in its most recent private round. The apples-to-apples comparison would be with the fully diluted value.

  • SpaceX is the current IPO record-holder, having raised $86.25 billion, although that included the greenshoe.

What we're watching: Shares are expected to begin trading today on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT."
 
 
2. New company, old guard
By Emily Peck
 

Illustration: Maura Kearns/Axios
 

Anthropic's stock market debut today signals the dawn of a new era in tech, with one complication: Amazon and Google, the key players of the current era, will own nearly 30% of Anthropic after it goes public.

Why it matters: The companies that AI was supposed to disrupt are among the biggest financial beneficiaries of its rise.

Catch up quick: Amazon and Google each invested in Anthropic when it was private, and their shares will convert to a special nonvoting class of stock when the model AI company starts trading today.

  • After the debut, Amazon will hold 14.7% of shares in Anthropic, per a filing earlier this week — and could exercise the right to convert more outstanding notes into stakes in the company.
  • Google will hold 13.7% — that includes the purchase of $10 billion in additional Anthropic stock through a private placement accompanying the IPO.
  • These are nonvoting shares, so technically that would limit the tech giants' influence.

3. Exclusive: Bots fueled outage conspiracy theories
By Sam Sabin
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios
 

Bot accounts have helped spread conspiracy theories about a wave of major tech outages over the last week, according to new research shared exclusively with Axios.

Why it matters: Purveyors of disinformation appear to be exploiting public anxiety over the outages and fragile infrastructure, amplifying suspicions of coordinated cyberattacks and government cover-ups.

  • While it's unclear who's behind these accounts, the pattern shows that when technology failures lack substantive explanations, bot networks will fill the void to manufacture panic.

Catch up quick: Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase, United, Workday, the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Security Agency each faced outages over the last week.

  • Then came the conspiracy theories: When the FAA grounded flights for four hours Friday, people were quick to assume it was tied to the rollout of an AI tool at the agency. Some also tried linking the widespread Microsoft outage to recent company layoffs.

Yes, but: There's no publicly established evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack, despite the theories circulating online.

  • Several companies have attributed their disruptions to technical problems, rather than malicious activity, including efforts to patch vulnerabilities to make software more resilient.
  • Downdetector data show that while the seven days through Monday saw the highest number of weekly outages in the last 12 months, longer-term patterns are far from unprecedented, as Axios previously reported.

By the numbers: Suspected bots accounted for roughly 30% of posts promoting conspiracy theories about several recent tech outages, according to data from social media monitoring firm PeakMetrics.

  • During Microsoft's outage, bots accounted for 26% of conspiratorial posts.
  • Bots accounted for 34% of conspiracy-related posts during Friday's Workday outage, compared with 27% of other posts.
  • Likely bot accounts also made up 31% of conspiracy-related posts about Bank of America's outage and 28% of posts linking Chase's outage to other disruptions.
  • PeakMetrics analyzed social media discussions surrounding six recent outages and classified accounts that were likely to be bots and conspiracy-related posts.

Threat level: Jessica Pratt, a spokesperson for PeakMetrics, told Axios that most of the bot activity is aimed at "gaming the platforms' algorithms" and that it sees some foreign influence within that — although the company could not detail precisely how many of the bots are tied to foreign state media and governments.

  • PeakMetrics also observed a "small number of foreign state media and state-aligned accounts in the conversation," Pratt added.

4. Exclusive: Corporations want say in AI rules
By Madison Mills
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Seven corporate giants are joining forces to give the businesses using AI a bigger voice in writing the rules around its deployment.

Why it matters: Corporate America wants a better seat at the AI regulation table in Washington, which has so far mainly offered seats to frontier AI and tech companies.

Driving the news: America's AI Deployer Council launched today, the group shared exclusively with Axios.

  • The coalition brings together FedEx, GE Aerospace, General Motors, JPMorgan Chase, Pfizer, John Deere and United Airlines.

What they're saying: Companies using AI can be left out of safety discussions even when they're responsible for managing the risks, John Bailey, an adviser to the council, told Axios.

  • One example of a challenge: AI companies have to report incidents to regulators, yet they're not required to relay that information to the businesses using the models, Bailey said.
  • "There's a gap right now where a lot of times the deployers are just left out of that chain ... even though the deployers are the ones that are still mitigating the risk on the other side," Bailey said.

Friction point: The group also hopes to make a stronger pitch on the benefits of AI to a public that has made its skepticism of AI increasingly clear, particularly through the latest election results.

  • "We need to do a better job. And I say that we as a collective, it's deployers as well as the AI developers, with surfacing the real benefits," Bailey said.

  • Pay raises and added equity took center stage during Nvidia's first all-hands without Jensen Huang. (Wired)
  • In a review, Bloomberg's Jason Schreier called "Grand Theft Auto VI" "an unparalleled technical and comedic masterpiece." We'll know soon whether the memes predicting bad news dumps during the release will be realized.
  • At the New York Times' DealBook Summit, Elon Musk said he's "not MAGA" and admitted he felt "pretty foolish" after spending nearly half a billion dollars to elect Republicans in the blue wave midterms. (Variety)
